report:
**Conclusion: the answer is probably yes, not no.** Offering HIV self-testing *in addition to* usual testing options increases the number of people who test, based on randomized-trial evidence.

The strongest evidence is a 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis of 13 randomized controlled trials: self-testing increased testing uptake versus standard services (risk ratio **2.09**, 95% CI 1.69–2.58; moderate-certainty evidence). Effects were seen across several delivery approaches, including facility, community, and partner distribution.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8271120/

An earlier systematic review focused on men who have sex with men and transgender people also found higher uptake (RR **1.45**, 95% CI 1.20–1.75) and more tests during follow-up.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7713313/

**Why your “no” intuition has some support:** more testing does not necessarily mean more newly identified infections. Reviews have found that self-testing may not raise the proportion of tests that are positive, and linkage to confirmatory testing and HIV care can be weaker in some populations—particularly female sex workers. Thus, self-tests can substitute for clinic testing or create follow-up gaps unless confirmatory-care pathways are made easy.  
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-020-01835-z

WHO’s summary is appropriately qualified: in facilities, self-testing may produce uptake comparable to or higher than standard testing, rather than guaranteeing an increase in every setting.  
https://www.who.int/news/item/22-07-2023-who-recommends-optimizing-hiv-testing-services
